Mucket (Actinonaias ligamentina) is a freshwater mussel species native to the Mississippi River drainage and the Great Lakes region, where it inhabits riffles and runs of medium-to-large rivers with stable gravel and cobble substrates. At a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], hatching from the fertilised egg occurs after approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days], a developmental period that aligns with the relatively slow embryogenesis typical of unionid bivalves. The newly emerged glochidium, the parasitic larval stage, possesses a minute shell that measures just 0.0254 cm [Lb = 0.0254 cm] along its longest axis, reflecting the extremely small size at which these larvae must attach to the gills or fins of a suitable fish host. The wet weight of these glochidia at the moment of release from the parent's marsupial gills is estimated at 0.00000053 grams [Wwb = 0.00000053 grams], a value derived from comparative studies on related species such as Elliptio complanata in Canadian populations, where the larval mass was similarly measured under controlled laboratory conditions. This minuscule birth mass underscores the substantial maternal investment required to produce thousands of such offspring.

Once the parasitic glochidial stage concludes and the juvenile mussel drops from its fish host to begin an independent benthic existence, the individual enters a protracted period of somatic growth. The time at which puberty is attained has been estimated at 1370 days since birth [tp = 1370 days since birth] under thermal conditions averaging 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C]. This represents a substantial juvenile phase lasting several years, during which the mussel must reach a shell length sufficient to accommodate reproductive organs. At the pubertal transition, individuals typically measure approximately 5.85 cm [Lp = approximately 5.85 cm] in total shell length, while their corresponding wet weight has been recorded at 25 grams [Wwp = 25 grams], a figure that includes the mass of both the calcareous shell and the soft tissues along with any environmental water retained within the mantle cavity. By this stage, the mussel has shifted from a predominantly filter-feeding lifestyle focused on rapid tissue accumulation to one that must balance continued growth with the energetic demands of reproduction.

The maximum shell length attained by Actinonaias ligamentina during its lifetime is substantial, with the ultimate total length of fully grown adults reaching 18.4 cm [Li = 18.4 cm], a size that places this species among the larger unionids found in North American freshwaters. Corresponding to this impressive linear dimension, the ultimate wet weight of a senescent individual can approach 1017 grams [Wwi = 1017 grams], a mass that incorporates the heavy, nacreous shell characteristic of long-lived freshwater bivalves. This large terminal body size results from sustained feeding over a long lifespan, with shell growth slowing once the animal reaches its maximum dimensions. In comparison to other members of the family Unionidae, the Mucket exhibits a relatively large maximum size, likely an adaptation to the stable, productive habitats it occupies where predation pressure on adults is low. The energetic demands of supporting such a large body are met through continuous suspension feeding on phytoplankton and detritus, although growth rates can vary considerably across the species' broad geographic range.

Reproductive output in this species is considerable, reflecting the large body size and extended lifespan that allow for repeated spawning events over many years. An individual female can produce an average of 4277 eggs per day [Ri = 4277 eggs per day] during the peak of the spawning season when water temperatures stabilize at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a rate that translates into an extraordinarily high annual fecundity when sustained over the several-week-long breeding period. This daily egg production, derived by dividing the maximum yearly fecundity by 365 days, underscores the reproductive strategy common among unionid mussels: the release of vast numbers of glochidia to compensate for the extremely low probability that any given larva will successfully encounter and attach to a compatible fish host. The timing of peak reproduction coincides precisely with the thermal conditions that also optimize glochidial development and metamorphosis, ensuring that larvae are released when host fish are most abundant. Such a high daily reproductive rate is energetically demanding and likely contributes to the observed deceleration in somatic growth among older, reproductively active females.

Longevity in Actinonaias ligamentina is exceptional among freshwater invertebrates, with the maximum recorded lifespan documented at 14965 days [am = 14965 days] under thermal conditions averaging 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. This longevity, exceeding 40 years, is characteristic of many unionid bivalves and is facilitated by a relatively low metabolic rate, a robust shell that provides protection from most predators, and the stable environmental conditions typical of the large rivers this species inhabits. The age-related mortality curve is likely to be Type I, with most individuals surviving to advanced ages before senescence eventually leads to physiological death following a period of declining reproductive output. Field surveys have recovered individuals of this species that were estimated to be over half a century old based on shell annuli counts, though the 14965-day value (14965 days) [am = 14965 days] represents the most reliable published estimate from mark-recapture studies conducted in the Ohio River basin at a temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. The combination of a long lifespan, delayed maturity at 1370 days since birth [tp = 1370 days since birth], and high fecundity places this species firmly within a slow life-history strategy typical of large, stable-habitat freshwater mussels at a temperature of 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C].
